questions.question: What is a store?
options: A place where only music plays
A place where buying and selling of things happen
It has no purpose
Only for entertainment
questions.explanation: A store is a place where buying and selling of things happen. Stores buy products and then offer them to customers.

questions.question: What is included in the price of a product in a store?
options: The item, transportation, storage, employees, and store operations
Only the product itself
Nothing specific
Everything is free
questions.explanation: The price of a product includes the costs of transportation, storage, store employees, and store operations.

questions.question: Chrumko walks past three different shops on his way home. Shop A has bright lights and friendly staff. Shop B is smaller and quieter. Shop C is far away but has lower prices. Why might Shop A charge higher prices than Shop C?
options: The products in Shop A are always better quality
Shop A spends more on lighting, decoration, and staff
Shop C's products are fake
There is no difference at all
questions.explanation: Different shops have different costs. Shop A's bright lights, decoration, and more staff are part of their operating costs, which may be reflected in higher prices.

questions.question: Put the following steps in the correct order of how a store transaction works:
orderItems: Items are scanned at the till
questions.explanation: A store transaction follows this logical order: select items, go to checkout, scan items, see total, and pay. Understanding this helps you know what to expect.

questions.question: Stores buy products directly from manufacturers and then sell them to customers.
questions.explanation: True - stores must first buy products from manufacturers or suppliers before they can sell them to customers.

questions.question: Chrumko buys bread for €2, milk for €1.50, and apples for €1. How much does he spend total?
questions.explanation: €2 + €1.50 + €1 = €4.50. Understanding how prices add up helps you manage your money at the store.

questions.question: Match each factor with how it affects store prices:
matchRight: The farther goods are transported, the more expensive they are
The store has to pay a salary to every worker
questions.explanation: Different shops have different operating costs based on location, employee numbers, and store appearance - all reflected in their prices.

questions.question: Which statement about store costs is FALSE?
options: Stores need to pay for heating and lighting
Store workers' salaries are included in product prices
Store rent is paid by the manufacturer, not the store owner
Transportation of products costs money
questions.explanation: It's false that manufacturers pay store rent. The store owner pays rent, which is why prices must cover these costs.

questions.question: What is a discount?
options: A reduction in price from the original amount
An increase in price
Completely free
A more expensive item
questions.explanation: A discount means a product costs less than before. Stores use discounts to attract customers.

questions.question: If something is on discount, you must buy it because you'll save money.
questions.explanation: False - just because something is on sale doesn't mean you need it. Buying items only because they're discounted can waste money.

questions.question: Chrumko goes to the shop to buy only a snack. He sees a discount on milk chocolate. What should he do?
options: Buy it right away
Buy everything
Think about whether he really needs and wants it
Never buy anything
questions.explanation: Chrumko should pause and think. He didn't plan to buy sweets and has some at home already. A discount alone isn't a good enough reason to buy.

questions.question: Which statement about discounts is WRONG?
options: A discount means the item costs less than before
You should always buy discounted items even if you don't need them
A good discount is only on something you truly want and need
Stores use discounts to attract customers
questions.explanation: It's wrong to always buy discounted items. You should only buy discounts on things you actually need.

questions.question: Which type of purchase should you avoid even if there's a discount?
options: Things you want but don't need
Things you actually need and will use
Anything that seems popular
Random items just because they're cheaper
questions.explanation: Avoid buying random discounted items. A discount is only good when you need the item anyway.

questions.question: A chocolate bar normally costs €3. It has a discount and now costs €2. How much do you save?
questions.explanation: €3 - €2 = €1 saved. But remember - this only matters if you actually need the chocolate!

questions.question: Match the discount scenario with the smart decision:
matchLeft: Item you don't need is 50% off
Item you already have at home is 20% off
matchRight: Don't buy - saving nothing if you don't need it
Don't buy - you already have one
Good idea to buy - real value for money
questions.explanation: Smart discount buying means understanding which discounts provide real value for your situation.

questions.question: Discounts are always worth taking advantage of, even if you don't really need the item.
questions.explanation: False - a discount is only valuable if you actually need or truly want the item. Otherwise, you're just wasting money.

Why do stores use colorful signs and big letters?
options: To make products look more interesting and attract attention
No reason
For decoration
It doesn't matter
questions.explanation: Stores use colorful signs and big letters to make products look more interesting and attract our attention.

questions.question: Chrumko sees a big yellow sign saying 'best value package at the best price'. What should he do?
options: Buy it right away because it's the best deal
Buy all the goods
Never buy anything
Look at the actual price and compare with other products
questions.explanation: Chrumko should look at the actual price and compare with other products. A big sign doesn't automatically mean the best deal.

questions.question: Marketing signs in shops are designed to help you find the absolute best price available.
questions.explanation: False - big signs are designed to catch your attention, not necessarily to show the best value. You need to compare prices yourself.

questions.question: Which is an example of a marketing trick stores use?
options: Giving the lowest price to everyone
Hiding prices from customers
Placing expensive products at eye level
Telling customers not to come back
questions.explanation: Stores strategically place products where they're most visible to influence what you buy.

questions.question: Which statement about marketing is FALSE?
options: Stores use colorful packaging to attract attention
Price signs are always 100% honest about the true value
Marketing tricks can influence what you want to buy
Comparing prices at different shops helps find better deals
questions.explanation: It's false that price signs are always 100% honest about true value. Marketing can make things seem more valuable than they are.

questions.question: Match marketing tricks with their purpose:
matchLeft: Bright colored signs with large numbers
matchRight: Make you trust the product more
Increase chance you'll pick it up
questions.explanation: Each marketing trick serves a specific purpose to influence your buying decisions.

questions.question: A new product has bright packaging and a celebrity's name on it. It costs twice as much as an unnamed product of the same quality. Should Chrumko buy it?
options: No, he's paying for packaging and the celebrity's name, not better quality
Yes, the celebrity makes it better
The celebrity guarantees quality
Price doesn't matter
questions.explanation: Part of the high price is for marketing and celebrity endorsement, not necessarily for better quality. Smart shoppers look past the packaging.

questions.question: Drag each marketing element to whether it affects the actual product quality or just the perception:
questions.explanation: Understanding what affects real quality versus perception helps you make smarter buying decisions.

questions.question: What is an impulse purchase?
options: A quick purchase without planning or thinking
A planned purchase
The best purchase
It never happens
questions.explanation: An impulse purchase is a quick purchase without planning. It happens when something catches our interest and we decide immediately.

questions.question: Where do impulse purchases often happen?
options: Only at home
They never happen
Everywhere equally
At the checkout, where small items are easily visible
questions.explanation: Impulse purchases often happen at checkout, where small items are easily visible and we get tempted by them.

questions.question: Chrumko stands at checkout with his mum. He sees colorful gum right by the till. What should he do?
options: Buy it right away, it's important to satisfy every craving
Buy all the gum so he has a stash
Wait a moment and think about whether he really needs it
Never buy anything, even if he actually needs the product
questions.explanation: Chrumko should pause and think. A brief wait usually stops impulse urges. He likely has sweets at home already.

questions.question: Waiting 30 seconds before buying something at the checkout can stop most impulse cravings.
questions.explanation: True - most impulse urges pass quickly if you wait. A brief pause often prevents unnecessary purchases.

questions.question: Chrumko buys a candy bar for €2 every time he goes shopping (2 times per week). How much does he waste per month on impulse buys?
questions.explanation: 2 times per week × €2 = €4/week. €4 × 4 weeks = €16/month. Small impulse purchases add up quickly!

questions.question: Match the emotion with the type of impulse buying that results:
matchLeft: Feeling sad after losing a game
questions.explanation: Emotions often trigger impulse purchases. Recognizing your feelings helps you resist the urge to buy.

questions.question: Stores place tempting items at the checkout to help customers remember what they forgot to buy.
questions.explanation: False - checkout placement is strategic. Stores know you're waiting and tempted, so they place items there to increase impulse sales.

questions.question: Chrumko has these emotions at the shop - drag each to whether it triggers impulse buying or not:
questions.explanation: Negative emotions (bored, sad) and positive celebration emotions often trigger impulse buying more than planned shopping does.

questions.question: Which statement about impulse buying is WRONG?
options: Impulse purchases happen at checkout more often
Waiting before buying stops most impulses
All small items should be bought at checkout
Emotions can trigger impulse purchases
questions.explanation: It's wrong to think all small items should be bought at checkout. You should only buy what you truly need.

lessons.lessonName: How to Make Your Own Decisions

questions.question: How can you tell if you want something because you need it?
options: Ask yourself: do I need it? Will I use it for a long time?
There's no need to think
Buy everything you see
It's all impulse
questions.explanation: It helps to ask: Do I need it? Will I use it for a long time? Is it worth spending money on?

questions.question: Chrumko goes to buy a notebook he needs for school. He sees a pen with colorful packaging. What should he do?
options: Buy it right away because it looks nice
Stop and think about whether he really needs it
Not buy the pen, but buy more notebooks instead
Not even buy the notebook, since that's probably just an impulse too
questions.explanation: Chrumko should pause and think about whether he really needs the pen.

questions.question: If you already have two working pens at home, you need to buy another one because it looks nice.
questions.explanation: False - a nice-looking pen is not a real need when you already have working ones at home. Looks don't change function.

questions.question: Chrumko makes the right decision by buying only the notebook and leaving the pen. Why?
options: The pen is never useful
He will never want a pen
Pens are worthless
A few days later he's glad he saved money for real needs
questions.explanation: Smart decision-making saves money! Days later, Chrumko is happy he resisted the impulse.

questions.question: Match each question with how it helps you shop smarter:
matchLeft: Is this the most expensive option?
matchRight: Irrelevant - others' choices aren't your guide
Helps you buy things with real value
Irrelevant - price alone doesn't show value
questions.explanation: The key question is whether YOU will use it regularly - that's what determines real value for you.

questions.question: Chrumko has €20. He needs a pen (€2), notebook (€5), and pencils (€3). He sees sneakers he wants (€15). How much will he have left after buying essentials?
questions.explanation: €2 + €5 + €3 = €10 needed. €20 - €10 = €10 left. Not enough for €15 sneakers. Good decisions require math!

questions.question: Which statement about smart shopping is WRONG?
options: Buying cheap items you don't need wastes money
Making your own decisions helps you spend less
You should buy what your friends have because they like it
Thinking before buying saves money
questions.explanation: It's wrong to buy things just because friends have them. Your needs and budget are what matter.

questions.question: Your own judgment is more important than advertising when making buying decisions.
questions.explanation: True - your brain and judgment are your best shopping tools. Use them BEFORE you buy, not after!

questions.question: Drag each factor to whether it should influence your buying decision or not:
dragLabels: Your actual need for the item
questions.explanation: Smart buying focuses on your real needs and budget, not on marketing or peer pressure.
